summary: A 1977 description of the NAME/FINGER protocol, which lets a user ask a remote host who is logged in or for information about a user. It was later replaced by RFC 1194, RFC 1196 and RFC 1288.

plainLanguage.summary: You ask a computer who is using it right now, and it replies with names. This was an early way to check that.

subtitle: A 1977 note describing how to ask a remote host who is logged in, or about one user, with a single line.

tldr.problem: Sites had programs giving friendly status reports on who was on the system or about a person, but no way to ask them across the network.
tldr.mechanism: The client connects to socket 117 octal (79 decimal), sends one command line ending in CRLF, and reads the report until the server closes the connection.
tldr.outcome: Later specifications RFC 1194, RFC 1196 and RFC 1288 replaced it.

today: RFC 742 was obsoleted by RFC 1194, RFC 1196 and RFC 1288. It is the early description of Finger.

sections.title: What NAME/FINGER Is
sections.content:
The Name/Finger protocol is an interface to the Name and Finger programs at several network sites. These return a friendly, human-oriented status report on either the system at the moment or one particular person in depth.

When written, only the SAIL, SRI and ITS sites supported it. There is no required report format; the protocol mostly specifies a single command line.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like asking the front desk "who is here right now?" or "is Ken in?" and getting a friendly answer.

sections.title: Using the Protocol
sections.content:
The client does an ICP to socket 117 octal (79 decimal) and sets up two 8-bit connections, sends a single command line ending in <CRLF>, and receives output. The server closes its connections when the output is finished.

A null line means the server should return a default report listing everyone using the system. A user name such as FOO asks for a report on only that user, whether logged in or not. ITS and SAIL allow several comma-separated names, and an ITS server returns fuller descriptions if the /W switch is given.
sections.plainLanguage: You send one line. A blank line means "who is here?" and a name means "tell me about this person".

sections.title: What the Reports Contain
sections.content:
The default listing should include at least each user's full name and the physical location of their terminal where it can be determined. Job name and idle time are also reasonable.

For a named user who is logged in, a line or two in the same format is returned. If not logged in, the expected reply gives the full name and time of last logout. There is also a plan feature, a short message the user leaves that is included in the response, perhaps read from a specially named text file.

If a name is ambiguous, all possible matches should be returned. SAIL lists the names only, while an ITS server gives full information for each.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer is a short card about each person: their name, where they are sitting and how long they have been quiet. People can also leave a note.

sections.title: Implementation Notes
sections.content:
Implementers are encouraged to contact the maintainers of NAME. The RFC suggests extending local programs to accept other sites, such as :NAME @SAIL on ITS.

A TIP or a simple Telnet user program may send meaningless option negotiations that can foul up the command line, so a server may filter out IAC bytes and respond negatively (IAC WON'T) to option commands. This is a convenience, not a requirement.
sections.plainLanguage: Some dial-in programs send extra chatter that confuses the answering computer, so it is allowed to ignore the chatter and say no.
